senses.en: a sudden violent shaking of the ground that can knock down buildings
examples: A strong **earthquake** hit the city early on Sunday morning.
Thousands of people lost their homes in the **earthquake**.
During an **earthquake**, get under a table and hold on.

earthquake.note: Stress the first part: **EARTH**quake. In news reports you may also see the shorter word *quake*, which means the same thing.

senses.en: a large amount of water covering land that is usually dry
examples: The **floods** last October destroyed most of the rice crop.
Heavy rain caused a serious **flood** in the north.
After the **flood**, mud was everywhere in our street.

senses.en: to fill a place with water, or to become full of water
examples: The river **flooded** the whole village in one night.
Our kitchen **floods** every rainy season.
The road was **flooded**, so the bus could not pass.

flood.note: Pronounced /flʌd/ — it rhymes with *blood*, not with *food*. The adjective is **flooded**: *a flooded street*.

senses.en: a long period of time with little or no rain, so that plants and animals suffer
examples: The **drought** lasted for eight months and the wells dried up.
Farmers lost their coffee plants in the **drought**.
Long periods of **drought** are becoming more common.

drought.note: Pronounced /draʊt/ — the *gh* is silent and the ending sounds like *out*. Do not confuse it with *draught* (a cold current of air).

senses.en: a mass of earth, mud and rock that falls down the side of a hill or mountain
examples: A **landslide** blocked the mountain road for three days.
Heavy rain often causes **landslides** in this province.
Two houses were buried by the **landslide**.

senses.en: a very large victory in an election
senses.vi: thắng lợi áp đảo (trong bầu cử)
examples: Her party won the election by a **landslide**.
It was a **landslide** victory for the young candidate.

landslide.note: The first meaning is the one you need in this unit. *Mudslide* is a similar word used when the material is mostly wet mud.

senses.en: an extremely large ocean wave, usually caused by an earthquake under the sea
examples: The **tsunami** reached the coast twenty minutes after the earthquake.
A huge **tsunami** swept away hundreds of small boats.
Sirens warned the villagers that a **tsunami** was coming.

tsunami.note: Pronounced /suːˈnɑːmi/ — the **t** is not pronounced in English, so it begins like *sue*. The word comes from Japanese. An older word for it, *tidal wave*, is not really correct because tides do not cause it.

senses.en: a mountain with a hole at the top through which hot melted rock, gas and ash come out
examples: Smoke rose from the **volcano** for several weeks.
There are more than a hundred active **volcanoes** in that country.
We climbed to the top of an old **volcano**.

forms.en: connected with or produced by a volcano
forms.ex: **Volcanic** ash covered the fields for miles.

volcano.note: The plural is **volcanoes** (with *-es*), though *volcanos* is sometimes seen. Note the stress: vol-**CA**-no.

senses.en: to suddenly throw out hot rock, ash and gas, used about a volcano
examples: The volcano **erupted** without any warning at midnight.
If that mountain **erupts**, the village must be evacuated.
Ash fell on the town for hours after the volcano **erupted**.

senses.en: to start suddenly and with a lot of force, used about noise, anger or fighting
examples: The crowd **erupted** in cheers when the team scored.
Fighting **erupted** in the streets after the announcement.

forms.en: the act of a volcano throwing out rock, ash and gas
forms.ex: The **eruption** lasted three days and covered the town in ash.

senses.en: to move people away from a dangerous place to somewhere safer
examples: The army **evacuated** two thousand people from the coast.
We were told to **evacuate** the building immediately.
Families were **evacuated** before the storm arrived.

forms.en: the act of moving people away from danger
forms.ex: The **evacuation** of the island took only six hours.

forms.en: a person who has been moved away from a dangerous place
forms.ex: The school is now home to two hundred **evacuees**.

evacuate.note: You can evacuate *people* or *a place*: **evacuate the residents** and **evacuate the hotel** are both correct.

senses.en: a place or building where people can stay to be safe from danger or bad weather
examples: The school was used as an emergency **shelter** during the flood.
Families slept in a **shelter** for two weeks.
We ran to a bus **shelter** when the rain started.

senses.en: protection from danger or bad weather
senses.vi: sự che chở, sự trú ẩn
examples: We took **shelter** under a big tree.
The victims need food, water and **shelter**.

senses.en: to protect somebody from danger, or to stay somewhere to be safe
examples: Hundreds of people **sheltered** in the temple that night.
The high wall **shelters** the garden from the wind.

shelter.note: When it means protection in general it is **uncountable**: *take shelter*, not *take a shelter*. When it is a particular building it is countable: *an emergency shelter*.

senses.en: to save somebody or something from a dangerous or harmful situation
examples: Soldiers **rescued** a family from the roof of their house.
The dog was **rescued** after two days under the rubble.
They used a boat to **rescue** people from the flooded village.

senses.en: the act of saving somebody from danger
senses.vi: cuộc giải cứu, sự cứu hộ
examples: The **rescue** took more than ten hours.
A **rescue** team arrived from the capital that evening.

forms.en: a person who saves somebody from danger
forms.ex: The **rescuers** worked all night in the rain.

rescue.note: Pronounced /ˈreskjuː/, with the stress on the first part. The *-ing* form drops the *e*: **rescuing**.

senses.en: physical harm caused to something, which makes it less useful or valuable
examples: The storm caused serious **damage** to the school roof.
There was little **damage** to the houses on the hill.
Engineers are checking the **damage** to the bridge.

senses.en: to harm something so that it does not work properly or look as good as before
senses.vi: làm hư hại, gây thiệt hại
examples: The flood **damaged** hundreds of motorbikes.
Strong winds **damaged** the roof but did not destroy the house.

damage.note: The noun is **uncountable** — say *a lot of damage*, never *many damages*. Compare with **destroy**: *damage* means to harm something partly, so it can be repaired; *destroy* means to ruin it completely.

senses.en: to damage something so badly that it no longer exists or can never be used again
examples: The fire **destroyed** three houses in less than an hour.
The earthquake **destroyed** the old bridge completely.
Thousands of trees were **destroyed** by the landslide.

forms.en: the act of destroying something, or the state of being destroyed
forms.vi: sự phá huỷ, sự tàn phá
forms.ex: The typhoon left a trail of **destruction** along the coast.
It was the most **destructive** storm in fifty years.

destroy.note: There is no noun *destroyment*; the noun is **destruction**. Remember the difference: a damaged house can be repaired, a destroyed house cannot.

senses.en: to fall down suddenly, used about a building, roof or structure
examples: The old wall **collapsed** during the second earthquake.
Part of the roof **collapsed** under the weight of the water.
Two bridges **collapsed** and the road was closed.

senses.en: to fall down because you are very ill, tired or weak
examples: One rescuer **collapsed** from exhaustion after twelve hours.
She **collapsed** in the heat and was taken to hospital.

senses.en: the sudden falling down of a building or structure
examples: The **collapse** of the bridge trapped several cars.
Nobody was hurt in the **collapse** of the old factory.

collapse.note: Stress the second part: col-**LAPSE**. As a verb it is intransitive — say *the roof collapsed*, not *the storm collapsed the roof*.

senses.en: a statement or sign telling people that something bad may happen so that they can prepare
examples: The government issued a flood **warning** for the whole province.
The storm arrived without any **warning**.
People ignored the **warning** and stayed in their homes.

forms.en: to tell somebody about a possible danger or problem
forms.ex: Radio stations **warned** people to leave the coast.

warning.note: After **warn** you often use a *to*-infinitive: *They warned us **to stay** indoors.* Note *without warning* has no article.

senses.en: a statement about what the weather or another situation will probably be like
examples: The weather **forecast** says there will be heavy rain tonight.
According to the **forecast**, the typhoon will reach us by Friday.
I always check the **forecast** before a long trip.

senses.en: to say what you think will happen in the future, using information you have now
examples: Scientists **forecast** stronger storms in the coming years.
Rain was **forecast** for the weekend, but the sky stayed clear.

forms.en: a person whose job is to say what the weather will be like
forms.ex: The **forecaster** on TV said the storm would turn west.

forecast.note: The verb is usually irregular: **forecast → forecast → forecast**. The form *forecasted* exists but is less common. Stress the first part: **FORE**cast.

senses.en: a person who has been hurt, killed or badly affected by an event or a crime
examples: The **victims** of the earthquake need clean water and blankets.
Most of the flood **victims** are living in temporary shelters.
A fund was set up to help the **victims** of the landslide.

victim.note: A **victim** is someone harmed by the disaster — they may or may not have died. A **survivor** is someone who lived through it. Someone can be both: *a victim who is now a survivor*.

senses.en: food, money, medicine and other help given to people after a disaster
examples: **Relief** arrived by helicopter three days after the flood.
Our school collected clothes for the **relief** effort.
**Relief** workers are still handing out rice and water.

senses.en: the good feeling you have when something unpleasant stops or does not happen
examples: It was a huge **relief** to hear that my cousin was safe.
She smiled with **relief** when the water finally went down.

relief.note: **Relief** is uncountable in both meanings — never *reliefs*. The related verb is **relieve** (note the different spelling and the /v/ sound).

senses.en: a person who is still alive after an accident, illness or disaster
examples: Rescue teams found three **survivors** under the fallen building.
The **survivors** were taken to a shelter near the river.
She was the only **survivor** of the landslide.

forms.en: to continue to live after a dangerous event
forms.ex: The family **survived** the flood by climbing onto the roof.

forms.en: the state of continuing to live after danger
forms.ex: Clean water is the key to **survival** after a disaster.

survivor.note: Note the spelling: **surviv-or**, not *surviver*. Stress the middle part: sur-**VI**-vor.

senses.en: a small but extremely strong storm in which the wind turns in a circle and travels across the land in a narrow path
examples: A **tornado** crossed the field and pulled up every young tree in its path.
The **tornado** lasted only four minutes, but it took the roof off the school.
Two **tornadoes** were reported in the same province on the same afternoon.

tornado.note: Plural **tornadoes**, with an *e*. Stress the middle syllable: tor-**NA**-do. A tornado crosses land in a narrow line; a huge turning storm that forms over the sea is a *typhoon* or a *hurricane*.

senses.en: a tube that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, used for pouring something into a small opening
examples: She poured the cooking oil through a **funnel** so that none of it spilled.
There is a plastic **funnel** in the second kitchen drawer.

senses.en: the funnel-shaped column of turning wind you can see when a tornado forms
examples: We saw a grey **funnel** of wind moving across the field towards the fence.
The **funnel** touched the ground for less than a minute and then lifted again.

funnel.note: Two *n*s, one *l*: **funnel**. Stress the first syllable, ˈfunnel, and keep the second one short and light.

senses.en: to shake slightly, in small quick movements
examples: The whole building **trembled** for about thirty seconds.
Books and lights **trembled** on the shelves, but nothing fell.

senses.en: to shake because you are frightened, cold or upset
examples: Her hands were **trembling** as she read the message from the village.
The little boy was **trembling** with cold when the boat reached him.

tremble.note: **Tremble** is small and quick; **shake** can be much bigger. A building *trembles* in a slight earthquake and *shakes* in a strong one. Vietnamese *rung* covers both, so choose by size.

senses.en: to move quickly from side to side or up and down
examples: Everything in the room began to **shake** just after midnight.
The old bridge **shook** every time a lorry crossed it.

senses.en: to hold something and move it quickly backwards and forwards
examples: **Shake** the bottle of medicine before you open it.
He **shook** the branch until the last of the fruit came down.

forms.en: the movement of something that shakes
forms.ex: The **shaking** lasted half a minute and then stopped.

shake.note: Irregular: shake – **shook** – **shaken**. ❌ *shaked*. Note the two nouns: *a shake* is one movement, *shaking* is the whole event.

senses.en: to say what you think will happen before it happens
examples: Scientists still cannot **predict** exactly when an earthquake will happen.
The weather service **predicted** three days of heavy rain, and it was right.
Nobody **predicted** that the river would rise as fast as it did.

forms.en: a statement about what you think will happen
forms.ex: Her **prediction** about the storm turned out to be exactly right.

forms.en: happening in a way you can know about in advance
forms.ex: Floods here are **predictable** — they arrive every October.

predict.note: **Predict** takes a noun or a *that*-clause, never *to* + verb: ✅ *They predicted that the storm would turn north.* ❌ *They predicted the storm to turn north.* Stress the second syllable: preˈdict.

senses.en: a small object that you blow into to make a loud high sound
examples: Keep a **whistle** in your bag so that you can call for help in the dark.
The rescue worker blew his **whistle** twice and waited for an answer.

senses.en: to make a high sound by blowing air through your lips or through a whistle
examples: The wind was **whistling** through the gaps in the door all night.
He **whistled** to his dog from the top of the steps.

whistle.note: The *t* is silent: /ˈwɪsl/, like *wissle*. Same silent *t* in *listen* and *castle*.

senses.en: a bag or box of things you may need immediately in a disaster, such as water, a torch, medicine and a whistle
examples: Every family in the village keeps an **emergency kit** by the front door.
We packed an **emergency kit** with rice, matches, batteries and clean water.
Check your **emergency kit** twice a year and replace the old medicine.

emergency kit.note: Countable, so it takes *an*: *an emergency kit*. *Kit* here means a set of useful things gathered for one purpose.

senses.en: a person whose job is to find and help people who are in danger after an accident or a disaster
examples: **Rescue workers** carried an old woman out of the flooded house.
Two **rescue workers** walked for a whole day to reach the village.
A **rescue worker** found the boy under the fallen roof.

rescue worker.note: Usually plural in news reports, because they work in teams. Stress the first word: **RES**cue worker.

senses.en: the set of numbers used to say how strong an earthquake is
examples: The earthquake measured 6.2 on the **Richter scale**.
Anything above seven on the **Richter scale** does serious damage.
Scientists gave last night's shaking a low number on the **Richter scale**.

richter scale.note: Always *on **the** Richter scale*. Capital **R**: it is the surname of the scientist who designed it. It measures the strength of an earthquake, so a temperature scale is never the right answer here.

senses.en: the people or organisations with official power in a place, such as the local government
examples: The local **authorities** told every family near the river to move upstairs.
Wait for a message from the **authorities** before you go home.
The **authorities** closed every school in the district for two days.

senses.en: the official power to give orders and make people follow them
examples: A rescue worker has the **authority** to close a road.
Nobody has the **authority** to reopen the bridge yet.

authority.note: In disaster news it is almost always plural and takes *the*: *the authorities*. Plural spelling **authorities** (*-y* → *-ies*). Stress the second syllable: auˈthority.

senses.en: to take something out of the ground, roots and all, by pulling hard
senses.vi: nhổ bật lên, kéo bật lên
examples: The wind **pulled up** two young trees in our yard.
We **pulled up** the small plants and moved them inside before the storm.
The water **pulled** several fence posts **up** out of the soft ground.

senses.en: to stop, used about a vehicle and its driver
examples: A lorry **pulled up** beside us and the driver shouted a warning.
The bus **pulled up** at the end of the flooded street and everyone walked.

pull up.note: Separable in the first meaning: *pull the tree up* and *pull up the tree* are both fine, but with a pronoun only one order works — ✅ *pull it up*, ❌ *pull up it*.

senses.en: not in the place where people expect, and not yet found
examples: Four fishermen are still **missing** after Saturday's storm.
The family reported their grandfather **missing** on Tuesday morning.
Rescue workers searched all night for the **missing** children.

senses.en: not there, when it ought to be
examples: Two pages are **missing** from this book.
There is a **missing** roof sheet on the classroom next door.

missing.note: The usual verb is **go missing**: *Three boats went missing.* Do not confuse it with *lost*: a person who is **lost** does not know where they are, while a person who is **missing** cannot be found by anyone else.

senses.en: with very great force
examples: The volcano erupted **violently** and sent ash twenty kilometres into the air.
The small boat was rocking **violently** in the waves.
The door shook so **violently** that two of us had to hold it shut.

forms.en: using or having very great force
forms.ex: A **violent** wind tore the roof off the market that night.
The **violence** of the water surprised everyone in the village.

violently.note: In a report about nature, **violently** describes force, not anger or fighting. Four syllables, stressed on the first: ˈvi-o-lent-ly.
